data.title: Zemianske Podhradie – Hradiská, a Lusatian culture hillfort in the Bošáca valley
data.excerpt: Hradiská above Zemianske Podhradie is the best known of the hillforts of the Bošáca valley: a Final Bronze Age site of the Lusatian culture, defended by a rampart with a timber front wall and a box-and-grillage framework built in two phases. Jozef Ľudovít Holuby walked its two enclosures in 1887 and left a vivid description of the ramparts and gateways as well as of the bronzes and spindle whorls collected there.
data.metaTitle: Zemianske Podhradie – Hradiská, a Lusatian culture hillfort
data.metaDescription: The best known hillfort of the Bošáca valley, of the Final Bronze Age (1000–700 BC), occupied by the people of the Lusatian culture.

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: A massive rocky ridge protected the hillfort from the north-west, an artificial rampart and a ditch on the other sides; the rampart contained a timber front wall and a timber box-and-grillage framework and was built in two phases.

keyFacts.label: The first enclosure
keyFacts.value: The highest-lying part of Hradiská occupied an area of about 15 yokes.

keyFacts.label: The second enclosure
keyFacts.value: The lower-lying, second enclosure had an area of about 20 yokes, inclined to the east.

keyFacts.label: Size of the dwellings
keyFacts.value: The ground plans of the dwellings most often measured 5.5 × 4.3 metres.

keyFacts.label: Protective terrain
keyFacts.value: The settlement was protected by the surrounding hills and ridges – Lisica from the south, the ridge of the Hradištné Vŕšky and the steep Hlohová hill from the north.

keyFacts.label: Bronze finds
keyFacts.value: The finds include a broken knife, a sickle, three pins, small arrows known as „rýliky“, nails, hoops, an awl and part of a brooch (fibula).

keyFacts.label: Spindle whorls
keyFacts.value: Ten clay spindle whorls (little wheels for spindles) of various sizes and shapes were found at the site.

keyFacts.label: The first investigator
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was first investigated by Jozef Ľudovít Holuby, who published his observations in 1887 in Slovenské pohľady.

timeline.title: Occupation in the Final Bronze Age
timeline.description: The hillfort was occupied by the people of the Lusatian culture. The fortified settlement was protected from the north-west by a massive rocky ridge, on the other sides by an artificial rampart with a ditch; the rampart was built in two successive phases, with a timber front wall and a timber box-and-grillage framework.

timeline.title: Brief occupation by the Púchov culture
timeline.description: The site was briefly occupied by the people of the Púchov culture.

timeline.title: Occupation by the Slavs in the Great Moravian period
timeline.description: In the Great Moravian period, as well as in the 10th century, the hillfort was occupied by the Slavs, as is proved by several finds – mainly sherds, but also metal objects. Given its strategic position, the hillfort may have had a watch function at this time.

timeline.title: Jozef Ľudovít Holuby documented the hillfort
timeline.description: Holuby was the first to investigate the site and described his observations in the study Náleziská starožitností v Bošáckej doline (Find spots of antiquities in the Bošáca valley), published in Slovenské pohľady, volume VII.

children.text: In the Bošáca valley, ancient peoples and later also the Slavs built several important hillforts, the remains of which can still be seen even today.

The best known of them is the site of Hradiská, of the Final Bronze Age (1000–700 BC). This hillfort was occupied by the people of the Lusatian culture. The fortified settlement – the hillfort – is protected on the north-western side by a massive rocky ridge; on the other sides by an artificial bank – a rampart – and a ditch. Progressive structural elements were used in building the rampart: a timber front wall and a timber framework arranged into a system of boxes and grillages, which held the massive bank together. The rampart was built in two successive phases. Of the internal layout, the most important are the ground plans of the dwellings, most often measuring 5.5 × 4.3 metres. The rich inventory of finds consists of numerous pottery and bronze products, evidence of local bronze metallurgy and especially of agricultural activity. The site was also briefly occupied at the turn of the era (the Púchov culture). In the Great Moravian period, as well as in the 10th century, the hillfort was occupied by the Slavs, as is proved by several finds of the 9th and 10th centuries, mainly sherds, but also metal objects. At that time, given the strategic position of the hillfort, a watch function may be considered for it. As at Martákova skala, this hillfort too was first investigated by Jozef Ľudovít Holuby, who wrote of it:

To the west of Zemanské Podhradie, on the eastern spur of the Carpathians which divides the Moravské Lieskové valley from that of Bošáca, lie the „Hradiská“, belonging to the cadastral area of Z. Podhradie. The name „Hradiská“ itself betrays that in that place there must have stood not one but several strongholds – not, admittedly, of masonry, the ruins of which adorn our Váh region – but enclosed by ramparts (entrenchments), and such there indeed were, as the mighty and extensive ramparts or entrenchments, evident in many places, prove. In the course of this summer too I walked these places, which are of particular interest to us, several times and examined them attentively. It would seem that the founders of those Hradiská chose this very place for their dwelling in the Bronze Age not without reason, for from the very summit of Hradiská the whole Lieskové valley can be surveyed to the west, while from the south they were sheltered by the hill called „Lisica“, though both to the right and to the left of Lisica an open view over parts of the Váh region lay before them; finally, however, from the north the very ridge of the Hradištné Vŕšky, and behind them the cone-shaped, steep „Hlohová“ hill, easily accessible only from the western side, protected the inhabitants of Hradiská from a sudden attack. The dense forests spreading all around (of which, admittedly, only insignificant remnants in the form of oak and hornbeam scrub now remain) contributed considerably to the safety of this settlement.
Along the very ridge of the hill which divides the Bošáca valley from that of Lieskové there runs

a rampart 2–3 feet high, overgrown with scrub, running from the north in a straight line towards the south and about 300 paces long, which at its southern end curves round towards the east and again runs in a straight line for about 100 paces. Here the rampart is broken for about eight paces, where there was evidently the entrance into the enclosure from the southern side, and the people call this place „the gateway“ to this day. The continuation of the rampart runs in the same direction towards the east again for about 80 paces, above that same slope which falls to the „Žľaby“ valley and is overgrown with old oaks. This rampart issues into two arms, of which the lower one falls in a south-easterly direction along the ridge of the hill for about 90 paces, while the other again curves round to the north for about 25 paces, where it is lost in the ploughland. Yet we have scarcely gone 120 paces when, in the same direction, we come upon the continuation of that rampart, where below it a ditch 2 feet wide and 1 foot deep has been dug, and it ends where it meets the ridge of Hradištný Vŕšek, which falls steeply into the valley on its northern slope. This ditch, together with its rampart, the people call „the road“, and they say that there too there was a gateway into the stronghold.
This bounded place
is the first and highest-lying part of Hradiská
and occupies an area about 15 yokes in size. Over this whole area one can see in places
a quantity of ancient sherds

, burnt clay, here and there bones, soil mixed with charcoal and ash, and especially by the said gateways a great quantity of slag or hammerscale. Outside this enclosure as well, on the south, on the fields called „Rolincová“, sherds and burnt clay are found in abundance, and
bronze arrows and pins have been found

. Through the frequent ploughing of the fields lying within this enclosure, the sherds are broken up more and more, so that larger pieces can only rarely be seen. Since iron ploughs were introduced here too in place of wooden ones, the ploughing goes deeper, and from afar one can already tell on the ploughland, by the darker colour of the soil, where ash, charcoal and burnt clay have been turned up in greater quantity.
The second, lower part of Hradiská

, is enclosed on the north by the continuation of the ridge of Hradištný Vŕšek, very steep and hard of access on its northern slope, which at its lower end, on the Hradiská side, is about 15 feet high, while on the north it falls steeply for about 100 feet to the Rešetárovec valley. This little hill has been dug level at its top and was certainly also fortified and inhabited, for even on superficial digging we come upon burnt clay, sherds and bones; and there, where the approach to it was from the eastern side, a rampart 2 feet high begins again and runs southwards for a good 100 paces as far as the steep slope falling into the Žľaby valley, from where two ramparts run almost parallel in an easterly direction for about 80 paces and are lost in the ploughland. The entrances into this second enclosure can be made out from the north-east, the north-west and from the south, where a fairly comfortable road leads up. This second enclosure covers an area inclined to the east, about 20 yokes in size. Also deserving mention is
Hradištný Vŕšek

, which bounds this second enclosure on the north. Two approaches up it can be made out, and above its northern slope a rampart. About midway up its southern slope a terrace can be made out, in which I dug up many sherds. On the fields of this second enclosure the soil is in places very much mixed with charcoal and ash and with larger and smaller pieces of burnt clay. From this place I have two pieces of melted bronze with a green patina.
Here we have so far found the greatest number of bronze objects and of various spindle whorls

(little wheels for spindles) of burnt clay and roughly made from old clay sherds. Just now, at the beginning of October, I came in one place, overgrown with juniper, upon very greasy soil heavily mixed with burnt clay, charcoal and sherds, where I shall still dig in the course of this autumn, for this place has not yet been broken up by the plough and for that very reason promises more finds than the ploughland.
On these three Hradiská we have so far found no iron tools, but
only bronze objects heavily coated with green rust (patina)

, and everywhere many varied clay sherds, a considerable part of which are of graphite (such as is not found anywhere in the whole neighbourhood) so pure that one can write with those sherds as with a pencil. On the largest pieces of those sherds it is clearly to be seen that they were made by hand only, and not on a potter’s wheel, as the primitive ornaments made with the fingers also prove. I have one strong, thick sherd on which a raised band below the rim, with dimples pressed in with a finger (not with wood or any other tool), serves as decoration.
Spindle whorls

(little wheels for spindles) of various sizes and shapes we have found there 10; two ornamented, two merely patted together from clay with the fingers, with a hole for the spindle pierced through the centre, and several pieces made from fragments of old pots. This last testifies to the great thrift or poverty of the owners of those spindle whorls (perhaps more than 2,000 years ago), since they could content themselves with such unadorned spindles. Whereas the spindle whorl is very handsome and fired from fine clay. Striking is
the quantity of red deer bones

, which are found here. These bones can be recognised by their lightness and by the striking porosity at the break. The thicker bones are split: so those first inhabitants loved not only roast venison, but consumed the marrow as well. Among the quantity of all manner of bones I was unable to distinguish any human ones. But that sherds and bones are found in abundance in the ramparts already mentioned seems to me to suggest that those ramparts are of later origin than the fragments of clay vessels found in them. Or was that settlement perhaps destroyed by fire and then renewed again and provided with a stronger rampart for safety? Who can guess that? Those places where there are deposits of hammerscale deserve thorough digging. It is not impossible that various tools may be found there, or even clay moulds into which bronze objects were cast. The people say that there were smiths’ forges there. That Hradiská was enclosed by a wall, even in part, or that masonry houses stood there, cannot be said; but if houses (and not perhaps tents) stood there, they could only have been of timber. For we know that it is not so long since houses, and even churches, were built of wood not only in villages and among the mountains but also in towns, and from Xenophon’s Anabasis we know that in Asia Minor even kings lived in wooden towers, or bastions. It may have been similar, indeed it can be asserted almost with certainty that it actually was so, at our Hradiská too in prehistoric times.
Of bronze objects
we have the following: one
broken knife, one sickle, one arrow

a tiny one, 1½ inches long and ¾ inch wide at the barbs, with which, if it was not steeped in poison, it would hardly have been possible to kill a man, and it could only have been shot into light, thin fur. These bronze arrows have long been known to our people under the name „rýliky“, and more of them were ploughed up and brought to children as playthings, and so were lost;
three pins

, one 5 inches long with a head as big as a good-sized pea, prettily hatched around; a second about 4 inches long with a flat head, hatched lengthwise and with a ring below the head; a third without a head, broken and scraped clean of rust, which, like several other pieces of scraped bronze, was brought to me by herdsboys; two nails with flat heads, one of which is hollow; one tiny, perhaps having served as a finger ring, and another broader, larger, but thin and beautifully patinated
hoop
; one sharp, bent at the point and, at the other end, where it was set into wood, thick and angular
awl

; 3 fragments of bronze as thick as a goose quill and bent, one of which had ornaments like enamel, which, however, are discernible only at one end, because its finder – a herdsboy – had it beaten with a hammer at the smith’s when he was testing whether it might not be gold?! – and the upper part of a brooch (fibula) in the shape of a large one bent back by one arm. These objects we have. But we hear with annoyance that
knives, arrows, bows, war hammers and all manner of „pieces“ were ploughed up there at Hradiská and lost, or else sold to Jews for a few kreutzers.
I also have one well-preserved tile, 5 inches in diameter, with a loop in the middle, ploughed up on the highest part of Hradiská.
Besides the clay spindle whorls (little wheels for spindles) there are also found there
small rings
fired from fine clay, smoothed, excellently preserved. These served as ornament and used to be worn
threaded on a cord, around the throat
. One such clay bead is indeed heavily worn at the edges of its hole, from which it may be concluded with certainty that it was worn for a long time. Of the six specimens we have, each is different.“
Sadly, as with the other Bošáca hillforts, this one too was looted by metal detectorists before archaeologists resolved to carry out a more detailed excavation here.
